about: Applied Knowledge Test Paper 1 (MBBS0084) is a 60-credit, Term 3 examination in UCL's MBBS Year 1, not a taught module. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue and Year 1 assessment document describe it as a 2-hour online integrated knowledge assessment worth up to 100 marks, mixing single best answer (SBA) and very short answer (VSA) questions, some with images, with no negative marking. The five-option SBA and five-word VSA limits in that document are stated for the formative papers in the CIF weeks; they are not restated for the AKTs. Together with Paper 2 (MBBS0085) it forms the end-of-year summative assessment, which tests applied knowledge across all Year 1 modules, including the Clinical and Professional Practice strands. This guide explains the paper and how to prepare; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What AKT Paper 1 is and how it is run
notes.body:
Applied Knowledge Test Paper 1 (MBBS0084) is an examination, not a taught module, so it has no syllabus of its own. It tests what you have learned across UCL MBBS Year 1.

What UCL's official pages say (2026–27)
- Module catalogue: an integrated knowledge assessment, taken in Term 3, worth 60 credits, assessed 100% by examination and open only to MBBS students.
- Format: a 2-hour online exam worth no more than 100 marks, with a mix of single best answer (SBA) and very short answer (VSA) questions, some of which may include images.
- The Year 1 Format of Assessments document (2026–27) says the summative assessment is an integrated written and practical assessment made up of two Applied Knowledge Tests: Paper 1 (MBBS0084) and Paper 2 (MBBS0085), each a 2-hour online paper of up to 100 marks in the same SBA/VSA format.
- There is no negative marking.
- UCL has since posted a revised version (v2, September 2026) of the Year 1 Format of Assessments, which this guide could not check. The details here come from the August 2026 version, so read the latest version on the Medical School website for any changes.
- For the formative papers in the November and February CIF weeks, the same document says each SBA has five options and VSA answers must be no more than five words. It does not restate these limits for the summative AKTs, so practise in that format but follow the instructions on the paper itself and the sample questions on Moodle.

What it is designed to test
- The papers assess ability across modules and disciplines, including the Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP) strands, not one module at a time.
- UCL says they aim to test intellectual and practical skills rather than simple recall of facts. Expect clinical or experimental scenarios in which you apply knowledge.
- They are blueprinted to the year of study, the MBBS Curriculum Map, and the GMC's Good Medical Practice and Outcomes for Graduates as relevant to this stage. A blueprint maps questions to curriculum areas so the paper samples the whole year fairly.

Where Paper 1 sits in Year 1
- The Year 1 programme page lists, in order: Introduction to Fundamentals of Clinical Science 1; Foundations of Health and Medical Practice; Infection and Defence; Circulation and Breathing; Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism; three Consolidation, Integration and Feedback (CIF) weeks; the Patient Pathway (Integrated and Community Care); the CPP modules; the UCLMS Toolkit; the Student Selected Component; and the two AKT papers.
- The CIF weeks in November and February include online formative papers in the same question styles. The February paper is a mock under exam conditions, which makes it the best rehearsal for the AKTs.

What the official documents do not tell you
- The catalogue and the Format of Assessments do not give the pass mark, the balance of topics in each paper, or resit arrangements. (The 2026–27 MBBS Mark Scheme adds that the AKT pass mark is set by standard setting using a modified Angoff method.) Do not rely on rumours: UCL directs candidates to its Examination Guide for Candidates, the Medical School's policies for MBBS assessments and the MBBS Mark Scheme. Sample questions are on the Assessment Unit Moodle site.

Exam tips: confirm the date, time, platform and rules for the online exam well in advance, and practise on the sample questions in the same format so nothing about the interface is new on the day.

notes.h: Answering SBA and VSA questions, including image questions
notes.body:
Both AKT papers mix single best answer (SBA) and very short answer (VSA) questions, and some include images. UCL's 2026–27 Format of Assessments states that there is no negative marking. It gives five options per SBA and a five-word limit for VSA answers for the formative CIF papers, but does not restate these limits for the AKTs, so practise in that format and read the instructions on the day.

Timing
- Two hours for up to 100 marks is a little over a minute per mark. Do a first pass answering everything you can quickly, flag the hard ones, and come back.
- Because there is no negative marking, never leave a question blank: an educated guess costs nothing.

SBA technique
- Read the last line (the lead-in) first so you know what is being asked: the mechanism, the most likely diagnosis, the structure involved, the next step, or the investigation.
- Read the stem actively, noting age, sex, timing, key positives and negatives, and any results. Predict the answer before you look at the options.
- Several options may be partly true; choose the best fit for this patient and this question. Watch qualifiers such as "most likely", "first", "most appropriate" and "least".
- If you are torn between two options, ask which one explains every feature in the stem.

VSA technique
- You must recall the answer with no cue, so practise retrieval, not recognition.
- Give one short, specific answer, spelled correctly (the formative papers set a five-word limit; check the instructions on the AKT itself). Do not list alternatives; check the MBBS Mark Scheme and the sample questions for how answers are judged.
- Answer exactly what is asked: if the question asks for a nerve, give the nerve, not the muscle it supplies.
- A useful drill is to cover the options of an SBA and answer it as a VSA.

Image questions
- Images may include anatomy specimens or diagrams, radiographs and other scans, histology slides, ECGs or data plots.
- Start by naming what you are looking at: the modality, view or plane, the stain or magnification, and which side is left and right.
- For radiographs, remember the density rule (air black, fat dark grey, soft tissue grey, bone white, metal brightest) and look for lost borders.
- For histology, decide the tissue type first (epithelium, connective tissue, muscle or nerve), then the organ, then any abnormality.
- For graphs, read the axes and units before the curve.

Integrated questions
- Many stems cross module boundaries. A breathless patient could test lung anatomy, gas exchange physiology, pathology (for example a pulmonary embolus), pharmacology principles, data interpretation, and communication or ethics. Ask yourself which discipline the lead-in is really testing.

Common mistakes
- Changing correct answers without a clear reason; spending ten minutes on one question; misreading "least likely"; answering a different question from the one asked; and in VSAs, giving vague or over-long answers.

Exam tips: rehearse the whole routine (lead-in, stem, predict, choose, flag) on timed blocks of mixed questions until it is automatic.

notes.h: Planning revision across the Year 1 modules
notes.body:
Because AKT Paper 1 is integrated, revision must cover the whole of Year 1 and the links between modules, not one module at a time.

Map what you need to know
- Use the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives and the MBBS Curriculum Map as your checklist. They are what the papers are blueprinted against.
- List the systems modules (Foundations of Health and Medical Practice; Infection and Defence; Circulation and Breathing; Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism), the vertical CPP strands (Anatomy and Imaging, Clinical Skills and Practical Procedures, Doctor as a Data Scientist, Pathological Sciences, Use of Medicines), and the other vertical modules (mental health, social determinants of health, communication, ethics and law, patient safety and professionalism), plus the Patient Pathway.
- Rate yourself red, amber or green on each objective, and spend the most time on red.

Use techniques with good evidence
- Practice testing (retrieval): self-testing with questions and flashcards strengthens memory far more than rereading or highlighting. A large review by Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) rated practice testing and distributed practice as the most useful learning techniques.
- Spaced (distributed) practice: revisit each topic several times with growing gaps, rather than cramming once.
- Interleaving: mix topics within a session (for example cardiovascular, renal and microbiology questions together), which mirrors an integrated paper and trains you to identify what each question is testing.
- Explain topics aloud, or teach a friend, to expose gaps.

Use your formative feedback
- The CIF weeks (November and February) include formative papers in the same formats. The February one is a mock under exam conditions. Analyse every error: was it a knowledge gap, a misread question, poor technique or a timing problem? Then schedule the fixes.

A possible timetable
- From the start of Term 3: a weekly cycle covering every module, with daily mixed question blocks and flashcard review.
- About four weeks before: full timed practice papers, then targeted review of weak areas.
- Final week: light review of high-yield summaries, sleep and routine. Avoid learning large new topics.

Integration practice
- Take one clinical scenario (for example a patient with heart failure) and work through it from every angle: anatomy and imaging, physiology, pathology, the principles of how the medicines work, data interpretation, communication and ethics.

Wellbeing
- Sleep, exercise and breaks improve memory consolidation and performance. If illness or personal circumstances affect your preparation, find out about UCL's extenuating circumstances process early and talk to your personal tutor or Medical Student Support.

Exam tips: measure progress by your scores on timed mixed question sets, not by the hours you spend reading.

The questions in this pack are practice in the formats of UCL's Year 1 formative papers (five-option SBAs and short VSA-style answers) on standard Year 1 physiology and biochemistry. They are not taken from UCL papers. The official pages do not list the content of each AKT paper, so use the Year 1 learning objectives to check coverage.

High-yield facts behind these questions
- Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. At rest in an adult it is roughly 5 litres per minute. Mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.
- The sinoatrial node in the right atrium is the normal pacemaker. The mitral (bicuspid) valve separates the left atrium and left ventricle; the tricuspid valve separates the right atrium and right ventricle.
- Carbon dioxide is carried in the blood mainly as bicarbonate ions. Carbonic anhydrase in red cells catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Smaller amounts are carried as carbamino compounds (bound to amino groups on haemoglobin and other proteins) and dissolved in plasma.
- Body fluids in a typical adult man: total body water is about 60% of body weight (about 42 L in a 70 kg man). About two-thirds is intracellular (about 28 L) and one-third extracellular (about 14 L). Of the extracellular fluid, about three-quarters is interstitial and one-quarter is plasma (about 3.5 L). Women and older people have a lower percentage of body water.
- Potassium is the main intracellular cation; sodium is the main extracellular cation, maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
- Insulin lowers blood glucose: it moves GLUT4 transporters into the membranes of skeletal muscle and fat cells, promotes glycogen, fat and protein synthesis, and suppresses gluconeogenesis. Glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone act against insulin (counter-regulatory hormones).

How to use the questions
- Answer each SBA before looking at the options, then check the explanation for why every other option is wrong. Distractors are built from common misconceptions.
- Answer the VSA items from memory in five words or fewer, as in the formative papers.
- Then write your own questions on topics you find hard; writing distractors is an excellent test of understanding.

Exam tips: for calculation questions, write the formula and units first; most wrong options in calculation SBAs come from unit slips or using the wrong formula.

questions.q: A healthy adult at rest has a heart rate of 75 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 80 mL. What is the cardiac output?
questions.why: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 75 × 80 mL = 6000 mL/min = 6.0 L/min. 6000 L/min keeps the number in millilitres but labels it as litres. 1.07 divides stroke volume by heart rate instead of multiplying. 155 adds the two numbers, which have different units. 0.6 L/min divides by 10 000 instead of 1000 when converting millilitres to litres.

questions.q: In which form is most carbon dioxide transported in venous blood?
options: Bound to the haem iron of haemoglobin
questions.why: Most CO₂ is converted in red cells by carbonic anhydrase to carbonic acid, which dissociates to H⁺ and bicarbonate; the bicarbonate moves into plasma. Dissolved CO₂ is only a small fraction. CO₂ does not bind to the haem iron, which is where oxygen binds; it binds to amino groups on the globin chains. Those carbamino compounds carry a substantial minority, but not most. Carbonic acid is only a short-lived intermediate that dissociates almost at once.

questions.q: In a healthy 70 kg man, approximately what is the volume of intracellular fluid?
questions.why: Total body water is about 60% of 70 kg, about 42 L, of which about two-thirds, about 28 L, is intracellular. 42 L is total body water. 14 L is the extracellular fluid (the remaining third). 3.5 L is plasma volume, about a quarter of the extracellular fluid. 10.5 L is the interstitial fluid, about three-quarters of the extracellular fluid.

questions.q: Which hormone increases glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue by causing GLUT4 transporters to move into the cell membrane?
questions.why: Insulin triggers translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane in muscle and fat, increasing glucose uptake and lowering blood glucose. Glucagon acts mainly on the liver to raise blood glucose through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Adrenaline also raises blood glucose, mainly by glycogenolysis. Cortisol raises glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis and reducing insulin sensitivity. Growth hormone is also counter-regulatory and tends to raise blood glucose.

questions.q: VSA practice (no more than five words each): (a) Name the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle. (b) Name the normal pacemaker of the heart. (c) Name the main intracellular cation.
UCL's Year 1 AKT papers are 2 hours long, worth up to 100 marks, and have no negative marking. Explain how each of these facts should shape your exam strategy.
markScheme: About 1.2 minutes per mark: aim for a steady pace and do not get stuck
Use a first pass for confident answers, flagging hard questions for a second pass
No negative marking: answer every question, guessing intelligently by elimination if needed
Keep a few minutes at the end to check that no question is left blank and that VSA answers are short and specific, within any word limit in the instructions
questions.modelAnswer: With 2 hours for up to 100 marks, I have only about 1.2 minutes per mark, so I would keep a steady pace and avoid spending several minutes on one hard SBA. I would do a first pass answering everything I am reasonably sure of, flagging difficult questions to revisit. Because there is no negative marking, a wrong answer costs nothing extra, so I would never leave a question blank: for SBAs I would eliminate the options I can and choose the best remaining, and for VSAs I would give my best single specific answer. I would leave a few minutes at the end to check that every question has an answer and that each VSA answer is short, specific and within any word limit stated in the instructions.
